evidence_quotes: Introduces the concept of parameter estimation using sample characteristics or statistics, distinguishing population characteristics (parameters, which are usually unknown) from sample characteristics (statistics, which are usually known).
Outlines the four properties of a "best" estimator according to R.A. Fisher: unbiasedness, consistency, efficiency, and sufficiency.
Covers generating narrow confidence intervals (confidence limits) that enclose an unknown parameter with a high probability.

LESSON ONE
 CONCEPT OF ESTIMATION

 1.1 Introduction

 In this lesson we introduce the concept of estimation and distinguishing between parameters
 and statistics. Two types of methods of estimation will also be discussed.

 1.2 Learning Outcomes

 By the end of this lesson the learner will be able to:

 1.2.1 Explain the concept of estimation of parameters using sample characteristics
 or statistics.
 1.2.2 Distinguish between point and interval estimations
 1.2.1 Concept of Estimation

 The objective of statistics is to make an inference about a population based on information

 contained in a sample. Most statistical inference procedures involve either estimation or
 hypothesis testing. This course looks at estimation.

 1.2.2 Point and Interval Estimations
 (i) Point Estimation
 A point estimation procedure utilizes the sample information to arrive at a single number or
 point that estimates the population parameter.
 If we let the value of some statistic say t(X 1, X 2, …Xn ) to estimate the unknown parameter,
 then t(X 1, X 2, …Xn ) is called a point estimator.
 (ii) Interval Estimation
 An interval estimation procedure makes use of the sample information to arrive at two
 numbers that are intended to enclose the parameter of interest.
 This is where two statistics t 1 (X 1, X 2, …Xn ) and t 2 (X 1, X 2, …Xn ) where t 1 (X 1, X 2, …Xn ) < t 2 (X 1,
 X 2, …Xn ) so that [t 1 (X 1, X 2, …Xn ), t 2 (X 1, X 2, …Xn )] constitutes an interval for which the
 probability can be determined that it contains the unknown parameter.
 In either case, the actual estimation is accomplished by an estimator. An estimator is a rule
 or formula that tells us how to calculate an estimate based on measurements contained in a
 sample. Most frequently, an estimator is expressed as a formula.

LESSON THREE

 Sufficiency and efficiency of an estimators

 3.1 Introduction

 This lesson looks at the sufficiency and efficiency properties of a good estimator.

 3.2 Learning Outcomes
 By the end of this lesson the learner will be able to:

 1.2.1 Define sufficiency and test whether an estimator is sufficient or not.
 1.2.2 Define efficiency and test whether an estimator is efficient or not
 3.2.1 Sufficiency

 Definition

 Let X 1, X 2, …Xn be a random sample of size n from a population having a random variable X

 whose pdf is of the form f(x,)which is known except the parameter is unknown. The
 statistic T=t(X 1, X 2, …Xn ) is said to be a sufficient statistics for if the conditional

 distribution of X given t does not depend on.

 That is if P(X=x/T=t) is independent of the parameter, then T is a sufficient statistic for the

 parameter.

 A statistic is said to be sufficient for  if it carries all information about  that is carried by

 the sample. We require an estimator to carry all information about whatever it is estimating

 that is originally contained in the sample. Intuitively, we would wish the estimator to carry
 all the relevant information in the sample regarding the parameter. That is it should be

 sufficient.

## 1. Linear model and objective

Least squares chooses model parameters to minimize the sum of squared residuals. For observations $(x_i,y_i)$, fit a straight line $y_i=beta_0+beta_1x_i+epsilon_i$, where $beta_0$ is the intercept, $beta_1$ the slope, and $epsilon_i$ the unexplained error. The residual is $e_i=y_i-(betahat_0+betahat_1x_i)$.

In matrix notation, write $y=X beta+epsilon$, where the $i$th row of $X$ is $(1,x_i)$ and $beta=(beta_0,beta_1)^T$. The least-squares estimate minimizes $S(beta)=(y-X beta)^T(y-X beta)$.

## 2. Normal equations and solution

Differentiating $S(beta)$ with respect to $beta$ and setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations $X^T X betahat=X^T y$. If $X$ has full column rank, $X^T X$ is invertible and $betahat=(X^T X)^(-1)X^T y$.

For a straight line, full column rank requires that the observed $x_i$ values are not all identical. If this condition fails, slope and intercept are not separately identifiable by this formula. With rank deficiency, use a generalized inverse or impose additional constraints, and acknowledge that the coefficient solution may not be unique.

## 3. Scalar formulas and interpretation

When there is variation in $x$, the slope is $betahat_1=sum_i(x_i-Xbar)(y_i-Ybar)/sum_i(x_i-Xbar)^2$, and the intercept is $betahat_0=Ybar-betahat_1 Xbar$. The fitted line passes through $(Xbar,Ybar)$, and the residuals sum to zero when an intercept is included.

Least squares minimizes squared vertical residuals in the response direction; it does not minimize absolute errors or perpendicular distances. Squaring gives large residuals extra influence. A fitted association is not, by itself, evidence of causation.

## 4. Statistical properties and assumptions

The algebraic least-squares solution does not require normally distributed errors. Under a linear model with zero-mean errors and a full-rank design, it is unbiased for $beta$; with homoscedastic uncorrelated errors of variance $sigma^2$, its covariance matrix is $sigma^2(X^TX)^(-1)$. Normality is additionally used for exact finite-sample normal-theory inference, not for deriving the minimizer.

If error variances differ or errors are correlated, ordinary least squares may remain computable but its usual covariance and efficiency claims need adjustment. Inspect residual patterns and influential observations before making inferential claims.

## 5. Computation checklist

Construct $X$ with a column of ones for the intercept, form $X^TX$ and $X^Ty$, and solve the normal equations using a stable linear algebra method rather than explicitly calculating a matrix inverse in numerical work. Then compute fitted values and residuals and verify that the dimensions agree.

Check the rank condition, distinguish coefficients from residuals, and state what assumptions support any claim of unbiasedness or variance. For a hand calculation, the scalar slope and intercept formulas provide a useful cross-check of the matrix result.

The model is $\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$, where

$$
X = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2
\end{pmatrix} , \qquad \boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix}
\beta_0 \\ \beta_1
\end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 3
\end{pmatrix} .
$$

The normal equations are $X^{\mathsf{T}}X\boldsymbol{\beta} = X^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y}$. Compute:

$$
X^{\mathsf{T}}X = \begin{pmatrix}
5 & 0 \\ 0 & 10
\end{pmatrix} , \qquad X^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
5 \\ 9
\end{pmatrix} .
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
5 & 0 \\ 0 & 10
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat{\beta}_0 \\ \hat{\beta}_1
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
5 \\ 9
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Solving gives $5\hat{\beta}_0 = 5$, so $\hat{\beta}_0 = 1$, and $10\hat{\beta}_1 = 9$, so $\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.9$.
Therefore the least squares fitted line is

$$
\hat{y} = 1 + 0.9x.
$$

The model is $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$, $i=1,\dots,7$.

In matrix notation:

$$
\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
$$

where

$$
X = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 6 \\
1 & -4 \\
1 & 10 \\
1 & 8 \\
1 & 4 \\
1 & 13 \\
1 & 2
\end{pmatrix}, \quad
\boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix}
\beta_0 \\
\beta_1
\end{pmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
20 \\
18 \\
6 \\
2 \\
13 \\
22 \\
5
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The least squares normal equations are

$$
X^{\mathsf{T}}X\boldsymbol{\beta} = X^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y}.
$$

Compute:

$$
X^{\mathsf{T}}X = \begin{pmatrix}
7 & 39 \\
39 & 445
\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
X^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
86 \\
436
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
7 & 39 \\
39 & 445
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
\beta_0 \\
\beta_1
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
86 \\
436
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Solving, the determinant is

$$
\det(X^{\mathsf{T}}X) = 7(445) - 39^2 = 3115 - 1521 = 1594.
$$

Hence

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^{\mathsf{T}}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y} = \frac{1}{1594} \begin{pmatrix}
445 & -39 \\
-39 & 7
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
86 \\
436
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

So

$$
\hat{\beta}_0 = \frac{445(86) - 39(436)}{1594} = \frac{38270 - 17004}{1594} = \frac{21266}{1594} = \frac{10633}{797} \approx 13.3413,
$$

and

$$
\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{-39(86) + 7(436)}{1594} = \frac{-3354 + 3052}{1594} = \frac{-302}{1594} = -\frac{151}{797} \approx -0.1895.
$$

Therefore the fitted least squares line is

$$
\hat{y} = 13.3413 - 0.1895x.
$$
